 Business ACA open enrollment begins with higher prices, fewer options
 The open enrollment period for 2027 health insurance coverage under the Affordable Care Act (ACA) opened yesterday in most states and runs through December 15.
 By Holly Van Leuven November 2, 2026 • less than 3 min read
 TOPICS: Business / Industries / Healthcare The open enrollment period for 2027 health insurance coverage under the Affordable Care Act (ACA) opened yesterday in most states and runs through December 15. Many enrollees face higher premiums and fewer options, according to the nonprofit KFF, which conducts national health policy research.
 Medical metallurgy: As in prior years, the ACA is grouping plans into four “metal” tiers—platinum, gold, silver, and bronze. The higher the tier, the higher the monthly premium—but out-of-pocket costs for care are lower. The inverse is true of the baser metal plans. And this year, even the “cheap” plans are pricier.
 Rayna Wallace, a policy analyst at KFF, provided this example: For a 40-year-old nonsmoker who enrolls in a bronze plan for 2027, the monthly premium will be $511 compared to $385 in 2025. That represents a 34% increase.
 What’s behind the price hikes? As with private sector health insurance, the marketplace’s price hikes are attributed to labor shortages, inflation, and underlying medical care costs getting more expensive. Costs have also mounted since Covid-era premium subsidies expired at the end of 2025.
 Members and insurers feel the pinch
 Premium increases vary widely by state. On the low end of the spectrum is Vermont, where the average increase is expected to be 3%. Arizona is at the high end, with an average increase of 28%.
 The negative loop caused by higher prices impacts insurers and members, and vice versa:
 KFF’s research found that the expiration of the enhanced premium tax credits affected the potential market size for insurers and the risk pool, as healthier members may be more likely to leave to save money.
 When fewer people participate, profitability goes down, and insurers may reconsider doing business with the marketplace.
 Additionally, people who drop plans can’t be sure of how much health insurance they will need in the future, potentially jeopardizing their health and their savings.
 Big picture: As of last week, 11 health insurers said they would wholly or partially exit ACA marketplaces next year. Cigna announced it would leave all 11 states where it has provided plans to over 350,000 ACA enrollees.— HVL
